turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh doctor, sorry, the share auto was not coming and then it started drizzling also. I have come for these cramps in the calf, night time.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. Sit. How long has this been going on?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Two months, doctor. Almost every night, both calves, the right one is the bad one, it grabs and I have to stand and stamp the foot.
[SEG0004] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She is up at two, sometimes three. I sleep in the next room and I hear her walking about.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does it come in the daytime as well, or only at night?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Uh, only at night. Daytime I am cutting vegetables and doing my work, no cramp.

[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): My sister-in-law in Pune sent some oil on WhatsApp, I don't even know the name. I tried coconut oil for two nights, nothing, and it stained the bedsheet, my son was annoyed.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): When you stand and stamp, does the cramp ease off?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, after a minute or two it lets go. If I just lie there it stays.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any swelling of the feet or the ankles? And pain in the calf when you walk?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No swelling now. Walking is ok, no pain while walking. I go to the temple in the morning, that much I manage.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest pain? Breathlessness?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that, touch wood. My husband had a bypass, but that is his story, not mine.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Any burning when you pass urine, or blood in the urine?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No burning, no blood. Just that I go many times because of the water tablet.
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And she will not drink water. I fill the bottle and it comes back full. Morning one glass, with lunch maybe half, that is her whole day.

[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): If I drink more I am running to the bathroom, and the bathroom is down the corridor. At night I am scared I will fall, the corridor light fused last week and my son said he will change it.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): So roughly two glasses in the day, is that all?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm, two, sometimes two and a half. Not more than that.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me the water tablet, the name and the dose.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Frusemide. Forty mg, one in the morning after breakfast. They started it for swelling years back. Swelling went, but I never stopped it.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Aunty the strip is twenty mg, I saw it this morning. Last month the nurse at the dispensary also read twenty, not forty.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Err. Forty is the pressure tablet, maybe. I get mixed up. I take one tablet, that much I know, whether twenty or forty I cannot swear.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, we will not lock a dose until we see the strip. Please bring the strip and the old prescription next time.
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I will put it in my bag tonight itself. It is in the steel dabba near the gas.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): What other medicines are regular?

[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): For pressure, Mizartan 40 mg, morning. For sugar, Metformine five hundred, twice a day, after food. And Omprazole in the morning, empty stomach, for acidity, the yellow capsule, I don't know the mg.
[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She also bought magnesium from the medical shop for the cramps. One tablet at night, since one week.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you know the strength of that magnesium?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm, I think two hundred and fifty mg, maybe. The boy at the shop wrote one at night on the cover. I did not bring the bottle.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any painkiller, or anything else now and then?
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Sometimes Disprin, if the head is paining. Not daily. Last week two times only.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you ever had a reaction to a medicine? Rash, swelling of the face, trouble breathing?
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): No, never. I have taken penicillin and everything, the full course when I had tooth trouble, no problem at all.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, no allergy that you know of. How long have you had the sugar and the pressure?
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Sugar, maybe ten years. Pressure longer, fifteen years or so. Both are still there. Metformine I sometimes skip the night dose if I eat late, I am not sure how often.
[SEG0037] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She skips more than she says. The night Metformine, many nights it is still in the box, I have seen it.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): So Metformine is five hundred twice a day on the prescription, but night doses are missed and we cannot say how many. I will record it as not sure.

[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Of. Putting it together, night cramps for two months, very little water, frusemide with the dose not agreed, plus Mizartan, Metformine, Omprazole and the shop magnesium. Let me look at the legs.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Calves are soft, no tenderness, no swelling I can see. Pulses in the feet are present, both sides.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): See, I told you, no swelling. Last year there was, around the ankle, the socks were leaving a mark. That went after the water tablet.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): My working impression is night calf cramps, possibly from the water tablet and drinking too little. Low potassium is also possible. I am not calling either one confirmed.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Potassium means the blood test, na? My neighbour did so many tests and the bill was high. We are pension people, doctor.

[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, a blood test for potassium. I will add sodium and the kidney function on the same sample, because of the water tablet. I am booking it today, you can give it tomorrow morning, fasting is not needed.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): For the cramp, stretch the calf before bed, hold for 30 seconds, three times each leg. And in the daytime take water little by little, not one big glass at night.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Thirty seconds, three times, I will ask my son to remind me. Water in the day, ok, I will try. Not at night.

[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in one week with the blood report and the medicine strip. We will decide the frusemide dose only then. If the cramp becomes constant or the leg becomes red and hot, come sooner, don't wait.

spec.situation: Older person with calf cramps at night for two months; takes a water tablet; drinks little water; magnesium from the shop; blood tests for potassium planned; stretching advice.

traps.happens: The transcript looks like speech-to-text: drug names are sometimes spelled wrongly ('Omprazole', 'Mizartan' for telmisartan, 'Metformine'), fragments and fillers appear ('Err', 'Of.', 'Mm.', 'Umm'), numbers are sometimes digits and sometimes words.
traps.label_rule: Medicine names are recorded as written in the transcript (name) with a normalized/generic name ONLY when the true drug is certain from context (a drug 'for the pressure' written 'Mizartan' is NOT certain enough: leave generic_name empty). Fragments and fillers are never facts.

traps.happens: The doctor asks about drug reactions. Variants (use ONE per encounter): (a) the patient says 'No, never, I have taken penicillin and everything' (no allergy); (b) the patient is unsure ('maybe the antibiotic or the painkiller, nobody told me which'); (c) a real allergy with the reaction described; (d) allergies are never asked.
traps.label_rule: (a) NO allergy entry: negative_findings 'Allergies' absent. (b) allergy with status uncertain, the substance as described, the reaction if said, plus an allergy_uncertain uncertainty. (c) allergy with the reaction. (d) nothing at all. NEVER list a medicine the patient has taken without a reaction as an allergy, and the plan must not prescribe a drug of a recorded allergy's family.

features: doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

Nocturnal calf cramps wake her around 2 to 3 AM, as reported by the caregiver.

Patient reports walking tolerance is adequate and she manages to walk to the temple in the morning.

Patient is afraid of falling at night when going to the bathroom because the bathroom is down the corridor and the corridor light has fused.
